title: Blessing the grandsons (Genesis 48)
hookLine: Jacob blesses Ephraim and Manasseh, whose names parents still use to bless children on Friday night

cards: Friday night, in Jewish homes that keep the custom, something happens right before dinner. The candles are lit, the table's set.
A parent puts their hands on a child's head, sometimes a squirming toddler, sometimes a teenager rolling their eyes, sometimes a grown child home for the weekend, and says a blessing.
For a son, it starts with two names that may surprise you. Not Abraham. Not Moses.

teach.h: I HAD NOT THOUGHT TO SEE THY FACE.
teach.b: Jacob is sick, near the end, his eyes dim. Joseph brings his two sons to him, Manasseh the older and Ephraim the younger.
And the old man says something that sums up his whole life: "I had not thought to see thy face; and, lo, God hath let me see thy seed also." He thought Joseph was dead, torn by a wild animal.
Now he's holding his grandchildren. Joseph places them carefully: the older at Jacob's right hand, the younger at his left.
Jacob crosses his arms. Right hand on the younger, Ephraim; left on the older. Joseph tries to fix it.
Jacob refuses: I know, my son, I know. The younger will be greater. It's the old pattern of Genesis, younger before older, Jacob before Esau.
But this time there's no stolen blessing, no fight. Manasseh doesn't storm off.

teach.h: GOD MAKE THEE AS EPHRAIM AND MANASSEH.
teach.b: Then Jacob says: "By thee shall Israel bless, saying: God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." And that's what Jewish parents who keep the custom still say. Why these two?
Some say they're the first brothers in Genesis who didn't fight each other. Others say they were born and raised in Egypt, far from home, and still stayed who they were.
For daughters, parents name the four mothers: Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah.

teach.h: THE LORD BLESS THEE, AND KEEP THEE.
teach.b: Then, for all of them, the old priestly blessing: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee; The LORD make His face to shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee; The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."

how: On Friday night, in homes that keep the custom, parents place their hands on their children's heads and bless them, sons with the names of Ephraim and Manasseh and daughters with Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel and Leah, followed by the priestly blessing from Numbers 6.

o: the younger grandson, blessed with Jacob's right hand
Rachel's youngest son, the one Jacob kept at home
Joseph's firstborn son, the elder of the two boys

games.q: what's inside the blessing — tap the pairs.
p: the younger, under Jacob's right hand

s: Jacob put his right hand on the older grandson
he crossed his arms and put his right hand on Ephraim, the younger.
parents still bless sons with the names Ephraim and Manasseh
on Friday night, from Jacob's words: God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh.
Manasseh and Ephraim fought over the blessing
no fight is recorded; some commentators say that's exactly why they're the blessing.

games.q: you're Joseph. your old father has crossed his arms, putting his right hand on your younger son. what do you do?
o: try to move his right hand to the older son.
games.why: Joseph tries to move it. Jacob refuses: I know, my son, I know. the younger will be greater.

practice: Think of someone younger in your life, your own kid, a niece, a student, a new coworker, and picture them clearly. If you pray, hold them in the old words: the LORD bless thee, and keep thee.
If not, think of one good thing you see in them, something true, and imagine saying it to them.

wordCard.voice: Ephraim, the younger grandson Jacob blessed with his crossing right hand, before his older brother. His name and Manasseh's became the blessing Jewish parents still give.

orig.note: Hebrew: God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh. the Friday night blessing for sons.

carryVoice: Your line: may you be like them. No fight is recorded, and the blessing is still given. Day seventy-five, done.
